newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: N.Korea sustains zinc sales despite Cargill snub.
newsitem.headline: N.Korea sustains zinc sales despite Cargill snub.

text.p: Famine-stricken North Korea sold a large parcel of zinc to South Korea during the second quarter while failing to honour a metal-for-wheat barter deal with U.S. grain giant Cargill, unification ministry data showed on Friday.
The communist country exported 7,348 tonnes of zinc ingots worth $9.8 million to its wealthy neighbor between April-June.

South Korea's total purchases of North Korean zinc totalled 12,623 tonnes worth $15.9 million in the first half of this year, slightly down from 13,676 tonnes worth $14.5 million in the same period of last year.

"I think they did that because they received considerable free aid from a number of countries and aid groups around the world and they decided the limited barter materials that they had, in this case zinc, they wanted to use in some other means," Micek said.
Micek added the door was still open to a fresh grain deal with North Korea.
North Korea's zinc sales totalled 3,912 tonnes in June, 2,206 tonnes in May and 1,230 tonnes in April.
In early April, North Korea and Cargill had reached an agreement to barter 4,000 tonnes of zinc worth $4 million for 20,000 tonnes of wheat with a similar value.
The barter deal fell apart in June, just before delivery.

Cargill Inc chairman Ernie Micek told reporters in Washington on Thursday the deal had foundered because of the volume of international food aid donated to North Korea, which prompted Pyongyang to sell its zinc elsewhere.
This compared with 5,275 tonnes worth $6.1 million in the first quarter of this year and 7,510 tonnes worth $8.0 million in the second quarter of 1996, the ministry's figures showed.
Traders said North Koreans preferred to do business with South Korean firms, who have a more understanding attitude to the North's erratic business practices.
Another attraction of North Korean zinc in South Korea is that it is exempt from a five percent import tax, which tends to compensate for the metal's poorer quality, they said.
One trader said gold and zinc were the only commodities that North Korea could offer in exchange for much-needed foods and fertilisers.
He said the North would aim to maintain its output of these two metals to earn hard currency even though it was struggling with serious shortages of electricity, ore and capital.
"The North seems to have been seeking more fertilisers as well as food during the first half, with the domestic harvests concentrated in the second half of the year," a trader said.
He added that international aid had sustained the economy during the early part of the year.
South Korean traders said the North would have severe difficulties in maintaining its metal production due to its dilapidated infrastructure and current drought conditions.

"This year's metal production is somewhat uncertain due to the drought, but normally the North has produced more zinc from May till August with stable (hydroelectric) electric power supply, helped by the summer rainy season," one trader said.
He said metal deliveries by the North normal took about two to three weeks after payment despite a shipping distance of only one or two days.
"Sometimes zinc delivery by the North takes about one month," he added.
"Last year, we paid in advance for the North's zinc, but we have shipped wheat flour and fertilisers this year."
